definition: a piece of land almost surrounded by water.
example: The class traced the outline of the peninsula on the map.
originNote: from words meaning almost and island
spellingTip: Remember penin- + -sula; only one n in the middle.

definition: a chain or group of islands.
example: Indonesia is a vast archipelago with thousands of islands.
originNote: originally referred to the Aegean Sea
spellingTip: The tricky middle is -pel-, not -pill-.

definition: the arrangement of natural and artificial physical features of an area.
example: The steep topography made road construction difficult.
originNote: writing or description of a place
spellingTip: Ends with -graphy, not -grafy.

definition: the science or practice of making maps.
example: Digital tools have transformed modern cartography.
spellingTip: Think carto- + -graphy with ph, not f.

definition: half of the earth or of a sphere.
example: Australia lies in the Southern Hemisphere.
spellingTip: Sphere keeps the silent h after p.

definition: relating to the equator or regions near it.
example: Equatorial forests usually have high rainfall year-round.
spellingTip: Keep the sequence equa-, like equal without l.

definition: an imaginary line of longitude running from pole to pole.
example: The Prime Meridian passes through Greenwich.
spellingTip: The middle is -rid-, not -red-.

definition: the distance of a place north or south of the equator.
example: Cairns is located at a lower latitude than Sydney.
spellingTip: Latitude has lati-, while longitude has longi-.

definition: the distance of a place east or west of the Prime Meridian.
example: Navigators relied on longitude to determine position.
spellingTip: Longitude starts with long-, like long lines on a globe.

definition: a very steep rock face or cliff.
example: The hikers stopped well back from the precipice.
spellingTip: It ends with -ice, not -iss.

definition: a long, steep slope or cliff separating two levels of land.
example: The road winds along the edge of the escarpment.
originNote: from a root meaning shoe or slope
spellingTip: Remember scar in the middle: es-carp-ment.

definition: a stream or river that flows into a larger one.
example: This tributary feeds into the Murray River.
originNote: from giving or paying to another
spellingTip: Ends with -ary, not -ery.

definition: the point where two rivers or streams meet.
example: The town developed near the confluence of two rivers.
spellingTip: Think flu like fluid, then add -ence.

definition: relating to soil or sediment deposited by flowing water.
example: The river plain is covered with rich alluvial soil.
spellingTip: Double l at the start, then -uvial.

definition: an area of high, fairly level ground.
example: The village sits on a plateau above the valley.
originNote: from a word meaning flat surface
spellingTip: French ending -eau sounds like oh.

definition: the layer of atmosphere above the troposphere.
example: Some weather balloons rise into the stratosphere.
spellingTip: Sphere ends with -phere, not -feer.

definition: a seasonal wind system associated with heavy rainfall changes.
example: The summer monsoon brought intense rain to the region.
spellingTip: Double o makes the long sound in monsoon.

definition: a tropical grassland with scattered trees.
example: Large herds migrate across the savannah each year.
originNote: from a word for treeless plain
spellingTip: Double n and end with -ah.

definition: a fertile place in a desert where water is found.
example: The caravan stopped at an oasis for fresh water.
originNote: from a word for fertile desert spot
spellingTip: Starts with oa-, not wa- or oha-.

definition: the tidal mouth of a river where fresh and salt water mix.
example: Mangroves thrive in the sheltered estuary.
spellingTip: Ends with -ary, and keep the tu before ary.

definition: relating to a river delta.
example: The deltaic region supports fertile farmland.
originNote: from delta, the Greek letter shape
spellingTip: The ending is -aic, not just -ic after delt.

definition: relating to or forming a peninsula.
example: The peninsular climate is influenced by surrounding seas.
spellingTip: Peninsular adds -ar to peninsula.
